title: Characterizing the Prevalence of Obesity Misinformation, Factual Content, Stigma, and Positivity on the Social Media Platform Reddit Between 2011 and 2019: Infodemiology Study
screen_reason: The stated aim is to quantify the PRESENCE of obesity misinformation on Reddit, and the paper reports a share of items classified as misinformation with a full denominator: 0.47% (3610/764,179) of obesity-containing sentences. It also reports the human-labelled share on the 2000-sentence training sample (4%). Although a machine-learning classifier is built, the paper is not a detection/benchmark paper — the classifier is the instrument for a prevalence estimate, and 'classifier' is an allowed ground_truth. Construct is CONTENT: the denominator is all sentences that EXIST in the corpus, not what anyone consumed or shared.

estimates.country: Not stated (platform-wide Reddit; US-based authors, Reddit userbase described as predominantly adult men in the US)
estimates.date: Top-level comments made between 2011 and 2019 (retrieved via Pushshift)
estimates.measure_type: % of obesity-related Reddit comment sentences classified as misinformation
estimates.denominator: 764,179 sentences containing 'obese' or 'obesity', drawn from 689,447 de-duplicated top-level comments on non-age-restricted subreddits, 2011-2019 (13,123 subreddits, up to 375,053 unique authors)
estimates.definition: An XGBoost multiclass classifier (trained on 2000 human-labelled sentences) assigned each sentence one of misinformation, fact, stigma, positivity or other; misinformation vs fact was defined by the human labellers 'in accordance with peer-reviewed guidelines identified by the American Board of Obesity Medicine and aligned with scientific literature'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation and factual content were distinguished in accordance with peer-reviewed guidelines identified by the American Board of Obesity Medicine and aligned with scientific literature [21]."
estimates.source_quote:
Results: After removing ambiguous sentences, 0.47% (3610/764,179) of the sentences were labeled as misinformation, 1.88%
     (14,366/764,179) were labeled as stigma, 1.94% (14,799/764,179) were labeled as positivity, and 8.93% (68,276/764,179) were
     labeled as facts.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Model Implementation and Feature Importance' (p. 6); also Abstract Results
estimates.ground_truth_detail: XGBoost with oversampled training data, best of 5 candidate models plus 2 dummy classifiers; test performance accuracy 0.69, weighted average precision 0.69, weighted average recall 0.69, weighted F1 0.63. Training labels came from 3 research assistants trained by obesity-medicine researchers who independently labelled 2000 random sentences; majority vote of 2 of 3 gave a label to 94% of sentences; Fleiss kappa 0.36 ('low', which the authors attribute to the kappa paradox).
estimates.moderator_quote: Consequentially, all analysis was restricted to only sentences containing the words "obese" or "obesity" (n=764,179 sentences across 689,447 comments after the removal of duplicates) to ensure that sentences included in the final analysis were related to the topic of interest.
estimates.notes: Confidence medium, not high: the value is a machine label with 0.69 accuracy / 0.63 weighted F1, trained on human labels whose Fleiss kappa was 0.36, so the point estimate carries real classification error; the authors themselves call it a lower bound ('the true amount of misinformation and stigma on the platform is likely higher than what is presented here') because the keyword filter dropped colloquial terms such as 'chubby' and 'fat'. The denominator INCLUDES the 86.78% of sentences labelled 'other' (ambiguous / not of interest), which is the correct all-items denominator for CONTENT. Corpus pools 2011-2019 with no year-by-year breakdown; year coded as the 2015 midpoint of that span. Country coded Global: the corpus is all non-age-restricted subreddits, with no national restriction.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: 3 research assistants trained by researchers with expertise in obesity medicine; hierarchical labelling with fact/positivity as default; majority-of-3 rule, 94% of sentences labelled; Fleiss kappa 0.36; no significant psycholinguistic difference between consensus and non-consensus sentences.

estimates.notes: Kept because it is the HUMAN-coded prevalence on a random sample of the same corpus and it differs from the classifier estimate by roughly a factor of 8 (4% vs 0.47%) — an adjudicator should see both, and this contrast is exactly the kind of instrument effect the review codes. definition_variant=true marks it as the same measure under a different instrument, not a different veracity threshold. Borderline because the exact denominator is not printed (94% of 2000) and the percentages are given as whole numbers only. If the review pools only one row per paper, the classifier row (3610/764,179) is the paper's headline; this row should not be pooled alongside it, since it is the same corpus measured twice.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) '87.2%' — the Discussion adds misinformation (0.47%) to 'other'/ambiguous (86.78%) to compare with a Facebook study. That is a cross-category sum and 'other' is not misinformation, so no row (R8, and the construct would be wrong). 2) 'over 50% of posts were either inaccurate or highly ambiguous' is cited from reference [57] (a Facebook bariatric-surgery study), not this study's data. 3) Keyword-validation figures (96% of 'obese'/'obesity' comments related to the research question vs 38% across all keywords; 7 true positives / 8 false positives out of 1000) are instrument-validation numbers, not misinformation shares. 4) Stigma 1.88%, positivity 1.94% and fact 8.93% are other content categories, not misinformation, so no rows. 5) No CONCENTRATION row is possible: subreddit counts (r/AskReddit n=97,540, r/fatlogic n=77,417 etc.) are counts of obesity-related comments per community, not a top-X%-of-sources share of misinformation, so R1 is not met. 6) No temporal breakdown is reported, so the 2011-2019 series cannot be collapsed to a dated point; year is the span midpoint. QUOTE FORM: the text file is a -layout rendering of a two-column print page, so column text is interleaved line by line; row 1's source_quote is the exact within-line fragment carrying the 4% value and the sentence continues with the single word 'misinformation.' on the next column line ('...5% were labeled as positivity, and 4% were labeled as | misinformation.').

rob.design: Infodemiology study of a near-census of Reddit text: all top-level comments on non-age-restricted subreddits 2011-2019 matching 45 obesity/diet keywords (26,575,493 comments), then restricted to the 764,179 sentences containing 'obese' or 'obesity' across 689,447 de-duplicated comments. No sampling of people and no response rate. Ground truth built from 3 trained RAs labelling 2000 random sentences (majority-of-3; 94% labelled; Fleiss kappa 0.36), used to train an XGBoost classifier (accuracy 0.69, weighted F1 0.63 on a held-out 20% test split) which then labelled the whole corpus. Authors state the estimate is a lower bound (keyword restriction, colloquial terms excluded), that misclassification is possible and assumed non-differential, and that Reddit's userbase (predominantly adult men) limits generalisability. Posts (image/video) and lower-level comments were excluded.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation and factual content were distinguished in accordance with peer-reviewed guidelines identified by the American Board of Obesity Medicine and aligned with scientific literature [21].
rob.item10_quote: After running the final XGBoost model with an oversampled training data set on the entire set of sentences, 3610 (0.47%) sentences were labeled as misinformation, 14,366 (1.88%) sentences were labeled as weight-related stigma, 14,799 (1.94%) were labeled as positivity, 68,276 (8.93%) were labeled as factual content, and the rest (663,128/764,179, 86.78%) were labeled as other.
